core_problem: There is an urgent need to quantitatively evaluate Large Language Models as agents on challenging tasks in interactive environments. Existing evaluation focuses on individual procedures and lacks a standardized, multi-dimensional benchmark for LLM-as-Agent reasoning and decision-making in real-world scenarios.
methodology_summary: We introduce AGENTBENCH, a comprehensive benchmark to standardize evaluation of LLMs as agents. It defines eight distinct environments of three types based on real-world scenarios, offering a practical testbed for a wide array of capabilities. A thorough evaluation of 29 different LLMs is performed using AGENTBENCH. An integrated evaluation toolkit grounded in a Server-Client architecture with modular and scalable design principles is introduced to enable easy customization of model assessments for any LLMs using HTTP protocol. Overall score is produced by first re-scaling each task's average score to 1 across all evaluated models and then averaging the scores across all tasks for each model.
empirical_results: Extensive testing over 29 API-based and open-sourced LLMs shows top commercial LLMs present strong ability of acting as agents in complex environments, with a significant performance gap versus many OSS competitors no larger than 70B. Typical failure reasons are poor long-term reasoning, decision-making and instruction following. Improving instruction following and training on high-quality multi-round alignment data can improve agent performance. Code training has ambivalent impacts on different agent tasks, improving some while harming others. Models referenced include gpt-4 (0613), claude-3 (opus), glm-4, codellama-34b-instruct, vicuna-13b-v1.5, llama-2-70b.
explicit_limitations: Database evaluation emphasizes the complete pipeline on authentic SQL interfaces, databases and query types rather than isolated translation or small-table QA; Success Rate is adopted as main metric. Evaluation prompt setup uses a two-role dialogue paradigm user and agent with conversation history (u0, a0, ..., uk, ak). Inference truncates history to keep token count of (u0, ar, ur+1, ..., uk) <= 3500, appending '[NOTICE] 2r messages are omitted.' into u0, which may omit earlier context.
